response:
Attention sinks are specific token positions — typically the first token or tokens receiving disproportionately high attention weights across many heads regardless of semantic relevance — that emerge as a structural artifact in transformers, apparently serving as a "garbage collection" mechanism so that softmax-normalized attention weights can sum to one even when no position is genuinely informative. The central question here is whether sink formation is an inevitable consequence of the softmax normalization constraint, or whether it is specifically provoked, shaped, or suppressed by the positional encoding scheme (RoPE, ALiBi, learned absolute, NoPE, etc.) and the particular fine-tuning objective (next-token prediction, RLHF, instruction tuning, long-context SFT with synthetic data). Beginners tend to treat sinks as a curiosity — a visualization artifact in attention maps — while experts worry that sinks actively compress or discard information that would otherwise inform the residual stream, and that this pathology scales non-linearly with context length, meaning a model that behaves well at 4K tokens can silently degrade at 128K not because it "forgets" but because sink dynamics shift under longer positional distances. The positional encoding angle matters because RoPE's decay of attention logits with distance can accelerate sink consolidation at far positions, while ALiBi's explicit additive bias creates different pressure on which tokens become attractors; the fine-tuning objective matters because RLHF reward shaping can inadvertently reinforce sink behavior if the reward model is insensitive to long-range retrieval failures.

At 4K tokens the raw attention logits for a given query span a relatively compact range, but at 128K tokens the effective "competition" across sequence positions means the logit variance increases — more positions are vying for attention weight, and the softmax denominator grows, pushing most weights toward zero and concentrating mass on whichever positions have the highest logits by even a small margin. RoPE directly touches pre-softmax logits because it encodes relative position by rotating query and key vectors in frequency-paired dimensions, and the dot product of a rotated Q with a rotated K decays as a function of relative distance via the inner product of the rotation matrices — meaning far-away tokens get a geometric penalty baked into the logit itself, not added post-hoc. This decay is not uniform: RoPE's lower-frequency dimensions retain coherence at longer distances while high-frequency dimensions decorrelate quickly, so at 128K the effective logit contribution from most semantic content at far positions is suppressed, leaving nearby tokens and positional outliers (like position 0, which has zero relative distance from itself in many implementations) with artificially inflated comparative logits. Su et al.'s original RoPE paper assumed a maximum context of around 2K–8K tokens; when models are extended to 128K via techniques like YaRN or LongRoPE, the frequency basis is rescaled, but imperfect rescaling leaves residual logit distortions that empirically concentrate sink mass at specific positions. ALiBi takes a different path — it adds a scalar penalty proportional to distance directly to the pre-softmax logit, which is more interpretable but creates a hard monotonic pressure that can make distant tokens nearly unreachable regardless of semantic content, potentially worsening sinks at a different positional locus than RoPE. The expert worry is that these encoding-induced logit distortions interact multiplicatively with context length: doubling context doesn't double the problem, it can square it, because you're both increasing the softmax denominator and increasing the fraction of positions that receive a distance penalty.

response:
The evidence leans toward routing-around rather than repair: analyses of LLaMA-2 long-context fine-tunes and the LongChat series show that Q/K weight norms shift modestly but the dominant adaptation is that specific heads — often in middle-to-late layers — develop strongly asymmetric attention patterns that effectively ignore positional decay by attending almost exclusively to a small retrieval-specialized window, while other heads absorb the "attend everywhere vaguely" burden. This is consistent with the "lost in the middle" phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023) where models fine-tuned on long context still show a U-shaped retrieval accuracy curve: the routing strategy works at endpoints but the residual stream never receives well-formed representations from mid-sequence positions, suggesting the Q/K matrices weren't retrained to overcome decay but rather the model learned to avoid relying on the damaged signal. YaRN (Peng et al., 2023) is the clearest attempt at actual repair — it rescales RoPE's frequency basis and introduces a temperature correction to the attention logits, explicitly trying to restore the pre-softmax logit distribution to something resembling the trained range; the fact that YaRN still needs continued pretraining on long-context data to work well implies rescaling alone is insufficient and some weight-level adaptation is necessary, but it's unclear how much is Q/K versus MLP or layernorm parameters. To distinguish repair from routing experimentally, you would freeze Q and K projection weights post-fine-tuning and probe whether far-token logits (pre-softmax, before any residual contribution) have actually shifted in distribution — if they haven't, and performance is preserved, routing is dominant; if freezing Q/K collapses long-context performance while freezing MLP weights does not, you have evidence for weight-level repair in the attention mechanism specifically. A cleaner surgical test is activation patching: run a long-context task, identify the layers where the model correctly retrieves a far token, then patch in the residual stream activations from a short-context run at the same token position — if performance degrades sharply, the residual stream is carrying compensatory information that isn't present in the base model's short-context representations, confirming routing-around at the stream level rather than repair of the Q/K dot product geometry.

The mechanism is plausible: a reward model trained predominantly on short, well-formed responses has no gradient signal that penalizes degraded long-range retrieval, so PPO will freely sacrifice those specialized heads if doing so reduces KL divergence cost or smooths the optimization landscape — the retrieval heads are effectively an unprotected resource. The attention entropy signature of damage would be a shift from a bimodal distribution — one sharp sink peak plus one or two retrieval peaks at semantically relevant far positions — to a unimodal high-entropy distribution where the head attends somewhat uniformly across all positions, which looks superficially "healthy" in aggregate statistics but represents complete loss of the retrieval function. Anthropic's research on attention head superposition suggests an additional failure mode: under multi-task pressure, a single head may be co-opted to serve multiple functions simultaneously, which in practice means its attention pattern becomes a blurred mixture of what were previously two distinct heads' behaviors — the entropy stays moderate but the head is no longer cleanly doing either job. You could detect this experimentally by tracking per-head attention entropy on a held-out long-context retrieval benchmark throughout RLHF training steps, specifically watching for heads that were low-entropy (below ~1.5 nats in a 4K context) before RLHF and cross a threshold during PPO updates — a sudden entropy jump in those specific heads, not correlated with general layer-wide entropy changes, would be the smoking gun for selective co-optation rather than global model drift.

The minimal additional measurement is the causal contribution of the head's output to the residual stream — specifically, the L2 norm of the head's value-weighted output vector (the term added to the residual stream after the attention-weighted sum over values), compared against a counterfactual where that head's attention is replaced by a uniform distribution. A sink head and a retrieval head can have identical low entropy, but a sink head's value vectors at the sink position are typically near-zero or lie in a subspace that is nearly orthogonal to the directions that matter downstream — meaning ablating the head or randomizing its attention changes the residual stream very little, while ablating a retrieval head produces a large residual stream perturbation at exactly the token positions where the answer lives. This is essentially the "head importance" metric from Michel et al. (2019) but applied not to overall task performance but to the local residual stream delta, which makes it unsupervised — you don't need labels, just the magnitude of the counterfactual difference. Concretely, at inference time you would compute for each head: the norm of (actual head output minus uniform-attention head output), and heads with low entropy but low counterfactual delta are sinks, while heads with low entropy and high counterfactual delta are retrieval heads; this requires one additional forward pass per head in the naive implementation but can be approximated efficiently using the gradient of the residual stream norm with respect to attention weights, which costs roughly one backward pass total. Nanda et al.'s work on induction heads used a structurally similar logic — identifying heads by their functional effect on downstream activations rather than their attention pattern shape — and found that this counterfactual residual norm cleanly separates head types even in cases where entropy and attention visualizations are ambiguous. The key practical advantage is that this measurement is local and online: you can compute it on any input at inference time without a probe dataset, a labeled corpus, or any assumption about what the model is "supposed" to attend to.

The pathology you'd create is real and has a name in the adversarial ML literature: Goodhart's Law applied to mechanistic proxies. The model would discover that the easiest way to maximize counterfactual residual delta is not to retrieve semantically relevant far tokens but to write large, high-norm vectors into the residual stream from arbitrary positions — essentially manufacturing noise with high L2 norm that satisfies the metric while carrying no useful information, analogous to how reward models trained on human preferences can be gamed by responses that are verbose and confident rather than correct. A concrete failure mode: the model learns to place high-norm "dummy" value vectors at position 0 or other fixed positions, attends to them with low entropy, and produces large residual deltas that register as "retrieval" while the actual semantic content of far tokens never influences the residual stream — this would be invisible to the delta metric because the metric only measures magnitude, not alignment with task-relevant directions. The fix requires composing the delta metric with a downstream coherence check — something like measuring whether the residual stream perturbation caused by the head is aligned with the directions that predict correct output tokens, which brings you back toward needing labeled data or at minimum a contrastive signal from the language modeling loss on held-out long-context examples. This failure mode is a specific instance of a broader problem in mechanistic interpretability-guided training: any scalar summary of a head's internal behavior that is differentiable will be optimized directly by gradient descent, and the model's capacity to find degenerate solutions that satisfy the scalar while breaking the underlying function it was meant to measure is essentially unlimited given sufficient parameters.

The most promising candidate is residual stream dimensionality concentration: a head's contribution is semantically load-bearing if the vector it writes into the residual stream lies in the high-variance subspace of the residual stream's empirical covariance matrix across a distribution of inputs — that is, it projects significantly onto the principal components that account for most of the residual stream's variance across tokens and contexts, independent of any specific prediction target. The intuition is that the residual stream's principal subspace is shaped by what the model has learned to care about across all tasks; a hollow high-norm vector manufactured to satisfy the delta metric will, with high probability, lie in the low-variance "null space" of the residual stream covariance because the model hasn't been trained to read from that subspace downstream — it's adding energy in a direction that no subsequent layer attends to or uses. Elhage et al.'s work on superposition provides indirect support: they show that features the model genuinely uses cluster in specific subspaces of the residual stream, and that interference between features is managed geometrically — implying that load-bearing contributions have a geometric fingerprint (alignment with the "used" subspace) that hollow contributions would lack. Concretely, you would compute the top-k principal components of the residual stream at a given layer across a large corpus, then measure each head's contribution vector's projection mass onto those components — a load-bearing head would have high projection mass onto the top-k subspace, while a hollow head would have high total norm but low projection mass, a signature you can compute without any labeled data or prediction targets. The limitation is that this subspace is not truly fixed — it drifts across layers and shifts somewhat with fine-tuning — but within a training run it is stable enough to serve as a reference, and you could maintain a running estimate of the covariance using an online PCA update that adds negligible compute overhead during training. This geometric criterion is also more robust to adversarial optimization than the raw delta norm because manufacturing a high-norm vector that also happens to lie in the empirical high-variance subspace requires the model to write in directions that are already semantically "occupied," which means it would be interfering with existing features rather than exploiting empty dimensions — a much harder optimization target.
